messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a twenty-four-year-old Vietnamese-American painter who presented for treatment approximately six weeks after leaving a relationship in which he had been physically abused by his male partner over the course of nearly a year. His PCL-5 score of 39 places him in the clinical range for PTSD, and across the intake and first two sessions a coherent and self-reinforcing picture of his difficulties has emerged.

The abuse was not a single incident but a pattern that accelerated in its severity. The episodes Minh describes most vividly tended to begin without clear warning — a delay in a text reply, a meal that wasn't ready — and would escalate into his partner grabbing him, striking him, and on several occasions pinning him against the wall of their shared apartment while he went completely still, unable to move or speak. He remembers the particular quality of light in that apartment: the yellowish overhead bulb in the hallway, the sound of a key in the door. These sensory details did not stay in the past. They followed him out.

Minh's memory of the abuse is fragmented in ways that cause him significant distress. Certain moments are rendered with excruciating clarity — the specific angle of his partner's face, the sensation of pressure on his collarbone — while entire sequences have gone blank, and he cannot reconstruct the order in which things happened. This disordered, incomplete memory means the trauma has never settled into a coherent narrative he can locate in the past. Instead, when something in his environment touches it, he does not remember what happened so much as re-enter it: the room tilts, his body tightens, and he is certain it is happening again. That quality of reliving feeds directly into a pervasive sense of present danger — the fragmented, non-sequential nature of the memory makes it feel unfinished, unresolved, as though the threat it encoded is still ongoing. And because the memory can be activated by almost anything — an unwanted thought surfacing during quiet moments at work, the ordinary uncertainty of not knowing what a sound means, a sense that someone is watching him — Minh lives in a state of near-constant low-grade vigilance that spikes without predictable warning.

The vigilance has become structural. The moment Minh enters any space — the hardware store where he buys supplies, a client's home, a coffee shop — he locates the exits before he does anything else. When a delivery is late or a client doesn't respond promptly, he does not register it as inconvenience; he registers it as evidence that something bad is already unfolding. At night, in the apartment he now shares with his current partner, he lies listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering. This sustained threat monitoring keeps his nervous system primed, which in turn makes the fragmented memories more accessible and more vivid: a hypervigilant brain, scanning for danger, finds the trauma wherever it looks, pulling forward the partial images and physical sensations that confirm what it fears. The elevated threat state also deepens his conviction that he is fundamentally inadequate — that a person with any real worth would not have been in that situation, would have left sooner, would not still be frightened. He has come to believe that the abuse happened because of the sort of person he is, and that belief, once established, makes the world feel more threatening still, because a person who deserves harm can expect to receive it.

These appraisals have quietly narrowed his life. Minh avoids the neighbourhood where his former partner lives, takes different routes to job sites, and has stopped going to a studio collective he once attended. He manages his sleep carefully, avoiding naps and staying up late to push past the hour when the nightmares tend to come. When he feels threatened — a raised voice on a job site, an unexpected knock — he freezes entirely, just as he did against that apartment wall, and afterwards feels humiliated by his own body's response, which confirms to him that he is inadequate. These strategies have not brought relief. The avoidance means he never processes what happened; the sleep manipulation means he is exhausted and his defences lower; the freezing leaves him feeling exposed and ashamed. He no longer feels he belongs in the art community he once loved, nor fully at ease with his current partner, who has noticed the distance and asked questions Minh cannot yet answer.

What finally brought him in was a moment at work — he was painting the interior of a private home and found himself unable to continue when the homeowner left the room and he heard, from somewhere in the house, the sound of a key turning in a lock. He stood motionless for several minutes, brush in hand, heart hammering, utterly certain he was back in that hallway. He wants, more than anything, to stop living inside that apartment. What he fears most is that he never will.
